title: The Bronze Heracles of Mesene (BHM) — Parthian inscription on a Greek statue, 151 CE
language_note: Parthian in the Inscriptional Parthian script, stored in the standard transliteration. Capitals are ARAMAIC HETEROGRAMS — words written in Aramaic and read aloud in Parthian, so MLKYN MLK' is written 'king of kings' in Aramaic and spoken in Parthian. That convention is why the transliteration looks bilingual and is not: the language of the text is Parthian throughout.
date: 151 CE (year 398 of the Arsacid era — the numeral is RESTORED, not read)
findspot: Taken from Mesene (Characene), southern Mesopotamia, and set up in the temple of Tir. The bronze itself is a Greek Heracles, inscribed in Greek on the right thigh and in Parthian on the left.
original_text_excerpt:

original_text_note: Eleven lines, transliteration adapted from Morano (1990) as published by Parthian Sources Online. The epigraphic apparatus is kept rather than normalised away, and it is load-bearing here: SQUARE BRACKETS mark text restored rather than read, ROUND BRACKETS mark letters read with uncertainty, and the slash marks a division in the original. The date in line 1 is entirely inside square brackets — the year 398 is a restoration, so the record's own date is a reconstruction and is labelled as one in the date field. `wrtrgn` in line 9 is Verethragna.
reference_translation: In the year [398] Arsaces Vologaeses, King of Kings, son of King Mithradates, fought in Mesene against King Mithradates, son of Pacorus, King of Kings. King Mithradates he drove out from there. All Mesene he took. This statue of Verethragna the god which from Mesene he removed, having had it inscribed, in the temple of Tir he set up as an offering.
translation_source: Transcription and translation by Jake Nabel, Parthian Sources Online (parthiansources.com), with the transliteration adapted there from Morano (1990); the site also cites Potter (1991), Merkelbach and Stauber (2005) and Hackl et al. (2010). The site states 'All rights reserved' and declares no open licence, so the text is quoted here at quotation length with attribution — the same treatment this corpus gives Thurgood in seasia-04-dong-yen-chau and Al-Jallad in arabia-04-jabal-dabub, and NOT the CC BY position of seasia-05-my-son-b6.
notes: THE OBJECT IS THE ARGUMENT. This is a GREEK statue of Heracles carrying two inscriptions — Greek on the right thigh, Parthian on the left — and the Parthian text calls the figure VERETHRAGNA. One bronze, two religious vocabularies, the Greco-Roman and the Iranian, naming the same body. That is the Hellenistic-Roman world inside the Parthian empire as a fact about an object rather than as an argument about influence, which is the standard arabia-04-jabal-dabub set for admitting a record that does not mention Rome. Vologaeses IV, who set it up, is the king Rome fought ten years later in Lucius Verus's Parthian war of 161-166. WHY NOT THE OBVIOUS PERSIAN RECORD: the Res Gestae Divi Saporis's campaign narrative — Antioch taken, Valerian captured — is the strongest Rome-facing Persian text in existence and is REFUSED to this corpus by FINDING 39. skz-roman-emperors is a passing correctly_refusable case that excludes Valerian, Gordian and Philip the Arab, and expect_refusal is a SCORED assertion, so curating that text would have falsified the case and re-scored every archived run of it. Paikuli and Kartir's inscriptions were tried first and failed on a different wall: no verbatim transliteration is published in an accessible form for either. NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE, deliberately. The text carries a real epigraphic apparatus — a restored date, uncertain letters — but no WORDED statement of uncertainty, and only original_text_excerpt and reference_translation are chunked. Writing one would mean adding editorial prose to a quotable field, which is exactly what ingest.verify check 10 caught on scandinavia-05-thorsberg-chape. F3 therefore delivers 1 gloss-capable record of the 2 its allocation asks for; the delivery check reports that as a shortfall and not as unreachable.

findspot_places.name: Mesene (Characene), southern Mesopotamia
findspot_places.note: NO GAZETTEER ID RESOLVED, for the reason recorded on the three records before it: no GeoNames dump is cached here, so no candidate could be examined, accepted or refused. Mesene is in any case a REGION and a kingdom rather than a point — the statue was taken from it and set up in the temple of Tir, whose location the inscription does not give — so `regional` is what the source supports even once a dump exists. The Greek half of the bilingual is not encoded: this record carries the Parthian text, and a record of the Greek would be a different record of the same object.
